_note: EXAMPLE FILE -- fictional voice bank for 'Jordan Doe'. Copy to voice_bank.json and write every entry in your own words; the generator selects entries by id and never rewrites them. Fields: labels (one-line headline under the name), summaries (60-90 words, first person; 'audience' tags choose which fit a posting), positions (one-sentence opinions; one is printed under the summary), anecdotes (60-120 words, real stories with a number and a lesson; cover letters pick two), openers/closers (cover-letter first and last lines; {company} and {role} are filled in). Keep ids stable. Avoid the phrases listed in BANNED_PHRASES in jobhunt/tailor/verify.py.

labels.text: Platform engineer for payments and compliance systems
Backend engineer who puts the guardrail in code, not the prompt
Integration engineer learning the claims and eligibility stack

summaries.text: I build and run the back-end systems that move money and prove it moved correctly. Eight years in regulated fintech taught me to design for the auditor as well as the user: every service I own has a replayable log, a reconciliation path and a runbook someone else has used. I like client-facing work when it ends in a working integration rather than a slide.

My recent work is on the boundary between language models and controlled systems. I have shipped a review gate that rejects generated change descriptions when the claimed controls do not hold, and I keep the enforcement in code where a prompt cannot talk it away. I want roles where that habit matters more than demo polish.

I come to healthcare payments from fintech payments, where I ran reconciliation for two million daily transactions. Claims, eligibility and remittance are new vocabulary for a familiar problem: many parties, strict formats, and money that has to balance at the end of the day. I learn domains by parsing their files first.

positions.text: A safety rule that lives only in a prompt is a suggestion; one that lives in a validator is a rule.
Recovery time is the metric that tells you whether an architecture is honest about failure.
Audit evidence should be a by-product of the pipeline, never a project of its own.

anecdotes.text: In 2022 our billing monolith dropped a night of invoices after a schema change, and recovery took six hours of hand-written SQL. I proposed the move to event-driven services on Kafka and ran the migration over nine months with no customer-visible outage. The next comparable fault, a year later, was replayed from the log in eleven minutes. The lesson I kept was that the replay path has to be exercised on ordinary days, so I made it part of every release.

Our first SOC 2 audit cost the team two weeks of screenshots. Before the second one I wrote a nightly job that pulls deploy records, access reviews and ticket links into a signed evidence bundle, about 400 lines of Python and a cron entry. The second audit took the auditors three days and raised two findings, both real and both fixed within the week. What I learned is that auditors are easier to work with when the evidence arrives in their format, not ours.

When we let a model draft change descriptions for our release notes, one in nine claimed a control that the diff did not implement. Rather than tune the prompt, I built a gate that parses each claim and checks it against the control registry, rejecting the description when the evidence is missing. Reviewers confirmed every rejection in the first quarter. The habit I took from it is to treat model output as untrusted input and put the check where it cannot be skipped.
